id: Dear One Absent This Long While

prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

It has been so wet stones glaze in moss; everything blooms coldly. I expect you. I thought one night it was you at the base of the drive, you at the foot of the stairs, you in a shiver of light, but each time leaves in wind revealed themselves, the retreating shadow of a fox, daybreak. We expect you, cat and I, bluebirds and I, the stove. In May we dreamed of wreaths burning on bonfires over which young men and women leapt. June efforts quietly. I’ve planted vegetables along each garden wall so even if spring continues to disappoint we can say at least the lettuce loved the rain. I have new gloves and a new hoe. I practice eulogies. He was a hawk with white feathered legs. She had the quiet ribs of a salamander crossing the old pony post road. Yours is the name the leaves chatter at the edge of the unrabbited woods.

prompts.L3:
Please expand the following bullet points into a complete, well-structured text:

- The speaker waits longingly for someone’s return amid a cold, rain-soaked landscape.
- Windblown leaves, a fox’s shadow, and daybreak repeatedly create false impressions of the expected arrival.
- The speaker imagines the cat, bluebirds, and stove sharing in the anticipation.
- Despite a disappointing spring, the speaker plants vegetables and finds consolation in the lettuce thriving in the rain.
- Alongside tending the garden, the speaker practices poetic eulogies while hearing the absent person’s name in the leaves.
prompts.L4:
Please expand the following two-sentence summary into a complete text:

Through rain-soaked seasonal imagery, domestic rituals, and repeated misrecognitions, the speaker portrays an anxious wait for an absent “you” while preparing for both renewal and loss. The beloved remains missing yet vividly present in nature and memory, revealing how hope and grief can coexist and sustain everyday life.
prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: May, June, She

outputs.L1:
It has been so wet that the stones gleam with moss; everything blooms coldly. I await you. One night, I thought it was you at the base of the drive, you at the foot of the stairs, you in a shiver of light—but each time, what revealed itself was leaves in the wind, the retreating shadow of a fox, daybreak. We await you: the cat and I, the bluebirds and I, the stove.

In May, we dreamed of wreaths burning on bonfires over which young men and women leapt. June makes its quiet efforts. I have planted vegetables along each garden wall so that, even if spring continues to disappoint, we can say that at least the lettuce loved the rain. I have new gloves and a new hoe.

I practice eulogies. He was a hawk with white-feathered legs. She had the quiet ribs of a salamander crossing the old pony post road. Yours is the name the leaves chatter at the edge of the unrabbited woods.
outputs.L2:
Rain has lingered until moss shines across the rocks, and every blossom opens beneath a chill. I am waiting for you. One evening, I mistook a figure near the driveway for you; then I imagined you below the staircase, and again within a trembling gleam. Each vision proved to be something else: wind-tossed foliage, a fox’s shadow slipping away, the arrival of dawn.

All of us anticipate you—the cat beside me, the bluebirds, even the stove. In May, our sleep filled with garlands set aflame on bonfires while young women and men sprang across them. June makes its subdued attempt. I have put vegetables beside every garden wall, so that if spring fails us again, we may still admit that the lettuce flourished in all this rain.

I own a fresh pair of gloves and a new hoe. I rehearse memorial words: He resembled a hawk whose legs were covered in white feathers. She possessed the hushed rib cage of a salamander moving over the old pony post road. At the border of the woods where rabbits no longer live, the leaves murmur your name.
outputs.L3:
The speaker waits with deep longing for someone’s return, surrounded by a cold landscape drenched in persistent rain. Every movement seems to promise the arrival they are hoping for: windblown leaves resemble approaching footsteps, the passing shadow of a fox suggests a familiar figure, and even the first light of day briefly creates the illusion that the absent person has come home.

In this state of anticipation, the speaker imagines that the entire household and natural world are waiting too. The cat appears watchful, the bluebirds seem alert to the expected return, and the stove offers its warmth as though preparing to welcome someone back. Yet spring proves disappointing, bringing little of the renewal or comfort it usually promises.

Despite this discouragement, the speaker continues to plant vegetables and tend the garden. The lettuce, flourishing in the steady rain, becomes a modest source of consolation and a sign that life can still persist amid grief and uncertainty. At the same time, the speaker practices composing poetic eulogies, suggesting an effort to confront the possibility of permanent loss. Even so, the absent person remains vividly present in memory: as the leaves rustle in the wind, the speaker hears them repeating the person’s name.
outputs.L4:
Rain-soaked seasonal imagery creates a world suspended between endings and beginnings. The weather suggests both decay and renewal: rain darkens the landscape, blurs familiar shapes, and deepens the speaker’s melancholy, yet it also nourishes the possibility of new growth. Within this uncertain atmosphere, the speaker waits anxiously for an absent “you,” reading every movement in the natural world as a possible sign of return. A sound, a shadow, or a change in light briefly becomes the beloved before revealing itself as something ordinary. These repeated misrecognitions show how longing reshapes perception, making absence feel almost tangible.

Against this emotional uncertainty, the speaker continues with domestic rituals. Everyday acts of cleaning, arranging, preparing, and tending to the home provide structure and purpose. They may be performed in anticipation of the beloved’s arrival, but they also resemble preparations for a permanent farewell. The speaker therefore inhabits two possible futures at once: one in which the absent person returns and life begins again, and another in which the loss must finally be accepted. Ordinary tasks become a way of holding these conflicting possibilities together.

Although the beloved never appears, they remain vividly present in memory, nature, and the speaker’s habits of attention. The surrounding world repeatedly evokes them, so that absence does not become emptiness but a different form of presence. Hope persists because return still seems imaginable, while grief persists because each false recognition confirms that the beloved is not there. Neither feeling cancels the other.

The text ultimately presents waiting as a way of living with unresolved loss. Hope sustains the speaker’s preparations and keeps the future open, while grief preserves the emotional reality of the relationship. Through seasonal change, domestic routine, and the constant transformation of ordinary sights into reminders of the missing “you,” the speaker reveals how renewal and mourning can coexist. Everyday life continues not because loss has been overcome, but because hope and grief together make endurance possible.
outputs.L5: She arrived in May, when the gardens were still deciding whether to bloom. By June, the roses had opened, the evenings had grown warm, and her laughter had become part of the house. She brought no promises with her—only a small suitcase and the quiet courage to begin again.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a lyrical prose poem about waiting for someone through an unusually cold, rainy spring, blending domestic life, gardening, animals, and thoughts of death.
counterfactuals.output:
All spring the rain kept finding new ways into the house: beneath the door, through the cracked caulking, down the chimney in black, medicinal drops. I set bowls under the leaks and listened to the rooms fill with small clocks. Outside, the lilacs held their breath. The daffodils bowed to the mud as if apologizing for having believed the calendar.

I waited for you by doing what could be done. I washed the cups. I folded the towels into warm, useless squares. I made soup from the last onions, their green hearts already dreaming in the dark. On the sill, tomato seedlings leaned toward the pale window, thin as questions. Each morning I turned them, and each evening they had turned back.

The cold stayed. Rain silvered the backs of the crows and darkened the horses in the lower field until they looked cut from wet stone. A fox came at noon, flame-colored and starving, and stood among the drowned tulips. We watched one another through the glass. I thought: everything alive is waiting for the door in the world to open.

In the garden, worms surfaced like pink roots. The pear tree flowered during a week of frost, reckless with white. I wrapped its trunk in old sheets, tucked straw around the lettuces, carried the basil indoors at night as if saving children from a war. Still, many things died quietly. Their deaths were soft collapses: stems loosening, petals turning transparent, nests emptied by weather. I began to understand how death can be less an arrival than a long season of not arriving.

Your coat remained on its hook, holding the shape of your shoulders more faithfully than memory. Sometimes I touched the sleeve while passing. Sometimes I spoke to the cat about you. She had no patience for sorrow; she slept on the clean laundry, hunted moths, and drank from the rain bowls as though the roof had opened solely for her.

By May, the days were longer but not warmer. I planted beans in soil cold enough to numb my hands. I pressed each seed into darkness and covered it, an act so close to burial that I had to sit back on my heels. Yet burial was also planting. This was the terrible tenderness of the earth: it received everything without promising what would rise.

I waited for your footsteps in the gravel, your key worrying the lock, your voice calling my name from the wet blue dusk. Instead, the gutters overflowed. Frogs sang from the ditch. A doe gave birth beneath the cedar and licked her trembling young clean under the rain.

Then one morning, without permission, the clouds thinned. Light entered the kitchen and lay across the table like a letter. The beans broke ground. The pear tree, against reason, held three small fruits.

I opened the windows though the air was still cold. The house exhaled. Somewhere beyond the fields, beyond weather, beyond whatever keeps one body from another, you were coming or you were not. I set two cups on the table anyway, and in the garden every leaf lifted its green face to the rain.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose an intimate letter to an absent beloved in poetic, surreal language. Include repeated mistaken sightings of their return, a cat, bluebirds, a stove, wet moss, vegetables, and improvised eulogies.
counterfactuals.output:
My love,

This morning I mistook the bluebirds for your return.

They struck the window one by one—not with their bodies, but with their impossible color—and for a moment the whole room filled with the blue coat you wore the winter the river froze around the boats. I ran to the door. No one stood there except the wind, holding a handful of wet moss like a damp green letter it had forgotten how to read.

Later, the cat lifted her head from the chair and stared into the hallway. You know the way she does, as if listening to a key turn in a lock buried miles beneath the house. I whispered your name. The stove clicked awake behind me. Again I thought you had returned, quietly, through the kitchen—already rolling up your sleeves, already asking what could be made from the crooked carrots, the bruised tomatoes, the onions sprouting pale antlers in their basket.

But it was only the stove, practicing its small red sunrise.

I have begun giving improvised eulogies for everything that leaves me. For the cabbage gone soft in the drawer: *You were a green planet, tightly dreaming.* For the spider the cat carried tenderly between her teeth: *You repaired the corners of the world and were paid in dust.* For yesterday: *You had your faults, but you contained their breathing.*

I have not yet composed one for you.

This afternoon, someone crossed the field wearing your walk. I knew it was you by the slight lean of the shoulders, as though moving always into weather. I followed until the figure became a scarecrow stitched from fog and old shirts. Beneath its feet, the ground shone with wet moss. Bluebirds perched along its arms, bright as small doors into another life.

I asked them where you were.

They answered by flying away.

Tonight the cat has curled beside the stove, guarding the vegetables as if they are sleeping children. The potatoes dream underground dreams. The beets keep their dark hearts hidden. The celery stands in a jar of water, slowly inventing a country where nothing beloved disappears.

Every sound becomes you: the kettle beginning to tremble, the house settling into its bones, a branch touching the roof. Each time, I rise. Each time, I smooth my clothes. Each time, I open the door.

My love, if you are lost, follow the bluebirds. If they lie, follow the smell of rain on wet moss. If the moss forgets me, follow the smoke from the stove, the one thin gray ribbon sewing earth to heaven. If heaven will not release you, listen for my ridiculous eulogies drifting upward:

*Here lies the silence before your footsteps.*

*Here lies the empty chair, faithful to the shape of you.*

*Here lies the door, which opened and opened and was never ashamed.*

I will keep mistaking the world for your return.

Come prove me right.

Yours, beyond every disappearance.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a haunting pastoral monologue in which a solitary speaker tends a rural home and garden while expecting someone who may never come back.
counterfactuals.output:
Every morning I unlatch the gate, though no one comes by the road.

The hinge has learned a cry like a small, hurt animal. I could oil it, but then I might not hear you arrive. So I let it complain into the quiet, and I leave the gate open while I work.

The house keeps your absence carefully. Your cup hangs from its hook. Your coat, green once and now the color of old moss, waits behind the door. In winter I shake the dust from its shoulders. In summer I search its pockets for moths. Once I found a burr caught in the lining and carried it outside as if it were a seed.

I planted it by the wall.

Nothing grew.

Still, there is plenty to tend. The beans climb their poles with blind green fingers. The cabbages fold their leaves over their hearts. Each evening I carry water from the well, two pails knocking softly against my knees, and the path remembers my feet. I speak to the tomatoes when I tie them up. I tell the hens not to wander. I warn the fox, though I have not seen him in years.

It is good to give orders to things that do not obey.

Beyond the orchard, the fields lie down beneath the wind. The grass turns silver, then green, then silver again, like the flank of some great sleeping beast. Sometimes I stand with the scythe in my hands and mistake the swallows for words you have sent me. They dip over the meadow, black letters I cannot read.

You said you would come back before the apples reddened.

That first autumn, I left the sound ones on the highest branches for you. They darkened there, sweetened, fell. In the nights I heard them striking the ground one by one.

The next year I made cider.

The year after that, vinegar.

Now the oldest tree has split, and in its hollow a pair of owls have made their home. At dusk they call across the garden, one to the other. I do not envy them. Envy is a weed with a deep root, and I have enough of those.

I have mended the roof three times. I have whitewashed the kitchen. I have buried two dogs beneath the elder tree and marked their graves with stones. The river has changed its course at the lower field. Children I once knew by name pass on the road carrying children of their own. They ask whether I am waiting for someone.

“No,” I tell them. “Only keeping the place.”

But after they are gone, I set a second bowl on the table.

At night the house settles around me. The beams knock. Ash shifts in the hearth. Mice make their small journeys behind the walls. Sometimes a step sounds on the threshold—plain as rain, plain as judgment—and I rise so quickly the chair falls backward.

There is never anyone.

Once, in late November, I saw a figure at the far end of the lane. The fog had taken the hedges and half the sky, but someone was walking toward the house with your slow, uneven stride. I stood in the yard without breathing. I watched until the figure became the old pear tree, bent under rooks.

I laughed then.

I frightened the birds.

Do you remember the blue room? I keep the shutters closed so the sun will not fade it further. The bed is made. Lavender lies beneath the pillow, though it has lost its scent. On the sill are the smooth stones we gathered from the river, back when the river ran where it was told.

Sometimes I sleep there, but never beneath the blanket. I lie on top, fully dressed, listening.

What would I say if you came?

I have rehearsed reproaches through seedtime and harvest. I have sharpened them on the whetstone. I have hung them in rows like tools. Yet I know I would forget every one. I would touch your face to see what weather had done to it. I would ask if you were hungry.

There is soup most days.

There is bread when the flour holds out.

There is always rosemary at the door, for remembrance, though it has grown wild and woody and pushes its roots beneath the step. Soon it will crack the stone. I should cut it back.

Tomorrow, perhaps.

Tonight the hills are dark before the sky. A pale mist gathers where the pasture falls away, and the sheep stand in it like stones in shallow water. I have lit the lamp in the front window. From the road, it must look like a single star fallen low.

You may be dead. You may have forgotten the turn beyond the mill, the hawthorn hedge, the gate that cries when opened. You may live in some bright place where no one waits and nothing needs mending.

But I will bank the fire.

I will cover the seedlings.

I will leave the gate unlatched.

And if the wind crosses the threshold in the night, cold and empty-handed, I will rise and say your name before I know better.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a short piece of contemporary nature prose with the cadence of an elegy, moving from May bonfires to June rain and ending with the absent person’s name whispered by leaves.
counterfactuals.output:
In May we built bonfires at the field’s edge, feeding them fallen branches, last year’s bracken, letters we could no longer bear to keep. Sparks rose into the young dark like a flock startled from sleep. Beyond the flames, hawthorn flowered extravagantly, white as weather, white as grief.

Then June came down in rain. It silvered the fences, filled the foxglove bells, laid every long grass blade against the earth. Paths vanished beneath nettle and mud. The river moved heavily between its banks, carrying petals, feathers, the small wreckage of nests.

I walked there alone, listening for what the season had taken. In the wet wood, the trees leaned close. Wind passed through them once, then again, and all the leaves whispered your name.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a dreamlike prose poem about grief and anticipation set in a rain-soaked countryside; use vivid animal metaphors, seasonal imagery, and the recurring phrase “I expect you.”
counterfactuals.output:
Rain combs the countryside with silver teeth.  
The fields lie down beneath it, dark horses breathing in their sleep,  
and every ditch carries a small, brown river toward the sea.

I expect you.

Beyond the orchard, winter crouches like a white fox,  
though it is only October, though apples still glow  
among the leaves like the hearts of vanished birds.  
I walk the lane where your footprints have filled with rain.  
Each one holds a trembling sky.

I expect you.

Grief follows me—a black dog with no master,  
mud on its ribs, thunder in its throat.  
Sometimes it runs ahead and disappears into the wheat;  
sometimes it presses its wet head against my hand  
as if I were the one being forgiven.

At dusk, the sheep gather like torn clouds.  
The barn lifts its red, wounded wing.  
Under the hedges, summer’s last crickets  
wind their tiny clocks toward silence.

I expect you.

Perhaps you will come with spring in your pockets,  
with nests and green rain, with the wild hare’s quick pulse.  
Perhaps you will rise from the flooded meadow  
wearing the moon like a pale mask,  
your voice full of swallows returning.

All night the house listens.  
The chimney is a lonely heron.  
The windows shiver like moths pinned to darkness.  
I leave the door unlatched, though the wind enters,  
though the rain steps softly from room to room  
in your old shoes.

I expect you.

Morning comes slowly, a wounded deer  
lifting its golden head above the hills.  
Mist grazes the furrows. The river uncoils.  
Every bare branch points somewhere beyond itself.

And there, where the road dissolves into weather,  
where autumn becomes winter, where sorrow becomes a gate,  
I stand with my hands full of rain—

I expect you.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
